nameStory: Golden corydalis gets its sunny common name from its bright yellow flowers that seem to glow like little golden treasures. It's also playfully called "scrambled eggs" because clusters of the small, irregularly-shaped yellow blooms can look remarkably like a pan full of fluffy scrambled eggs from a distance!
description: Golden corydalis is a delicate annual wildflower that produces cheerful clusters of bright yellow, tubular flowers. This member of the poppy family typically grows 6-16 inches tall with finely divided, lacy leaves that give it an airy, delicate appearance. The plant has a somewhat sprawling growth habit and produces distinctive pea-pod-like fruits that are about 3/4 inch long.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers are tubular with an irregular shape and a distinctive spur at the back, clustered at the stem tips and blooming from spring through summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Delicate, finely divided leaves that feel soft and feathery to the touch, giving the plant a lacy, almost fern-like appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Narrow, pea-pod-like capsules about 3/4 inch long that hang from the stems and split open when ripe to release small, shiny black seeds

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that spreads in a somewhat sprawling manner, rarely exceeding 16 inches tall, with multiple branching stems

habitat: Golden corydalis thrives in disturbed soils and open areas throughout New England, including rocky slopes, sandy shores, and cleared woodlands. It particularly favors well-drained soils and can often be found in areas where the ground has been recently disturbed by construction, erosion, or natural events.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin blooming in late spring, with the first bright yellow flower clusters appearing as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with abundant golden flowers and active seed pod development throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Mature seed pods split open to disperse seeds, and the annual plant begins to die back as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground plant material remains, but seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Despite being in the poppy family, golden corydalis produces no milky sap like its famous relatives - instead, its stems contain a watery, slightly bitter juice that was traditionally used by Native Americans as a mild pain reliever.
confusionNotes: Golden corydalis might be confused with wild mustards or other small yellow wildflowers, but its distinctive tubular flowers with backward-pointing spurs and delicate, fern-like leaves set it apart. Remember: if it looks like scrambled eggs with lacy leaves, you've found your corydalis!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "golden smoke" fool you - this plant won't produce any actual smoke! The nickname likely comes from the hazy, delicate appearance of its finely divided foliage, which can create a soft, smoky visual effect when viewed from a distance.
compareHints: Golden corydalis is quite rare in New England compared to its relatives, with only 8 recorded observations. Unlike the more common pale corydalis species that have whitish or pale yellow flowers, golden corydalis displays distinctly bright, saturated yellow blooms. Its annual growth habit also differs from some perennial corydalis species that return from underground tubers year after year.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bird-in-a-bush differs from other New England Corydalis species mainly in its spring ephemeral nature and tuberous root system.

Unlike the more robust Yellow Corydalis with its coarser leaves and bright yellow flowers, incised fumewort has much more finely divided, delicate foliage and typically produces pink to purple blooms.
Yellow Corydalis differs from its corydalis cousins by its bright yellow flower color - most other corydalis species in our region have pink, purple, or white flowers.
Noble Corydalis stands out from other New England corydalis species by its larger size, bright golden-yellow flowers (rather than pink, purple, or pale yellow), and more robust growth habit.
Hollowroot differs from other New England corydalis species primarily in its early blooming time and the distinctive hollow tuber (though you shouldn't dig to check this).
Among the Corydalis species, Fern-leaved Corydalis stands out for having the most finely-divided, fern-like foliage - other corydalis have more substantial, less delicate leaves.
